meta.title: Danish C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Danish → English (see the Danish, recall the meaning) and English → Danish (see an English meaning, recall the Danish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words of Danish for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express themselves fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Danish has examinations at these levels — Prøve i Dansk 1, 2 and 3 and Studieprøven — but none was found to publish a word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 62 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — academic and intellectual life, society and governance, the economy and business, law and ethics, mind and behaviour, language and rhetoric, the abstract nouns of analysis, the verbs and adjectives of formal argument, and formal connectors — and the other 1438 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Danish, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 955 nouns are printed with their article — en or et — because the article is the gender, which decides the noun's definite ending, the adjective's ending and the pronoun that stands for it, and they show their definite singular and their plural (bilen, biler); the 288 verbs show their present, their past and their perfect with its auxiliary (spiser, spiste, har spist; går, gik, er gået), since Danish chooses between have and være by the verb, and behind the All forms fold their imperative, -s forms and participles. Real example sentences come with 863 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 369 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
